task.description:
SECURITY-REVIEWER hard gate (WF-02 Step 2c) on REQ-168's implementation (Letflow.Engine.Wasm.MemoryGuard). REQ-168's own text explicitly names SECURITY-REVIEWER as a hard gate. This is the highest-stakes WASM implementation so far: its failure mode is a BEAM-node crash, not a request-level error, if a malicious guest's pointer/length pair ever reaches Wasmex.Memory unvalidated. Read the approved design (lib/letflow/design/req168-wasm-memory-isolation.md) and the real shipped code (lib/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard.ex) in full before verdict.

IMPORTANT -- ELIXIR-DEV flagged, rather than silently resolved, a real discrepancy between the design doc's own worked example table (section 5.2) and the algorithm as literally specified (section 2): for check_bounds(2^63, 2^63, 65536), the design's table expected {:length_exceeds_memory, ...} but the algorithm's step 3 (offset-range check) fires FIRST since the offset alone already exceeds memory_size, correctly yielding {:offset_out_of_range, ...} instead. ELIXIR-DEV implemented the algorithm exactly as specified (not the table), which is the correct call, and added a second test case to still demonstrate the end-of-range/non-wraparound property the table's example was trying to show. Verify this reasoning yourself: confirm the shipped check_bounds/3 correctly implements section 2's algorithm step-by-step, and confirm no case exists where the actual implemented order of checks could let a dangerous magnitude slip through to a live Wasmex.Memory call under any input, regardless of which specific error atom it reports.

SAFETY REMINDER: this design found that wasmex can SIGABRT the whole OS process at extreme magnitudes (>= ~2^40). If you write any live-verification probes yourself, NEVER call read/4, write/4, or any Wasmex.Memory function with such a magnitude -- confirm the bounds-check algorithm's correctness through the PURE check_bounds/3 function and code reading, not by deliberately trying to trigger the dangerous path live.
acceptance_criteria: Confirm check_bounds/3's actual implementation matches design section 2's five-step algorithm exactly, and that Elixir's arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic is genuinely used throughout (no native-sized integer coercion, no Kernel functions that could truncate/wrap a bignum) for the offset+length computation.

Confirm read/4 and write/4 genuinely call check_bounds/3 (or equivalent) BEFORE ever calling any Wasmex.Memory accessor -- no code path reaches a live Wasmex.Memory call with unvalidated offset/length.
Confirm read/4 and write/4 fetch Wasmex.Memory.size/2 FRESH on every call (never cached, never passed in stale) -- read the real code, not just the design's claim.

Confirm the ELIXIR-DEV-flagged design-vs-table discrepancy is genuinely benign: verify no input exists where the implemented check-ordering (offset-range check before end-of-range check) could produce a false ACCEPT that the table's originally-expected ordering would have correctly rejected -- this is the one place a subtle ordering bug could theoretically create a real safety gap.

Confirm read/4 and write/4 pattern-match both the documented success shape and an {:error, _} tuple explicitly on every Wasmex.Memory call, per the design's section 1.6 finding that three of Wasmex.Memory's own @specs are incomplete -- confirm no unguarded pattern match exists that could crash on an unexpected {:error, _} return.

Confirm no test anywhere in the new test file calls a live Wasmex.Memory function (through read/4, write/4, or directly) with a magnitude >= 2^40 -- re-verify this yourself by reading every test case's literal arguments, do not trust ELIXIR-DEV's self-report alone given the stakes.

Cross-check against docs/agents/instructions/security-invariants.md INV-1..INV-8 explicitly -- INV-3 (untrusted-runtime sandboxing) and INV-8 (typed error handling / no unguarded crashes) are both squarely this diff's subject matter.
CRITICAL: the handoff's top-level status field (line 9) must be exactly PENDING/IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED/FAILED/ESCALATED/CANCELLED when you finish -- run mix letflow.lint_handoffs before finishing.

result.summary:
SECURITY-REVIEWER gate on Letflow.Engine.Wasm.MemoryGuard (REQ-168) -- PASS. Independently read the approved design (lib/letflow/design/req168-wasm-memory-isolation.md) and the shipped code (lib/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard.ex, test/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard_test.exs) in full; did not trust ELIXIR-DEV's self-report alone.

INV-1 (tenant data isolation): NOT-APPLICABLE. `git diff main...HEAD --stat -- priv/repo/migrations/` is empty; this diff touches no Ecto schema, migration, or tenant-scoped table. MemoryGuard operates purely on a Wasmex.StoreOrCaller.t()/Wasmex.Memory.t() handle a caller already holds -- no tenant data model involved.

INV-2 (server-side field authorisation): NOT-APPLICABLE -- no API response/serialization path touched (S4 not started).

INV-3 (untrusted-runtime sandboxing): APPLIES (updated finding -- decision 0014 is decided and S5 requirements REQ-165..168 are underway, so this invariant is checkable now, not deferred; same staleness pattern this file's INV-1 note already documents). Satisfied: MemoryGuard adds no new host-capability surface and does not touch capability/import-allowlist logic (`grep -n capability lib/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard.ex` = no hits; CapabilityGate/ModuleRegistry/PluginHandler are unmodified per `git diff --stat`). It is a defensive bounds-check layer sitting strictly below where capabilities are already gated -- it narrows what a guest can reach (rejects out-of-range and pathological-magnitude pointer/length pairs before any dereference) and grants no ambient network/filesystem/host-function access. No regression against the allowlist model.

INV-4 (secrets by reference only): APPLIES (live today). `grep -rniE '(password|secret|client_secret|token)\s*(=|:)\s*"[^"]{8,}"' lib/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard.ex test/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard_test.exs` = no hits. No secret material anywhere in this diff.

INV-5 (not-found/forbidden indistinguishability): NOT-APPLICABLE -- no lookup-by-ID endpoint (S4 not started).

INV-6 (new data-access paths prove scoping): satisfied by this handoff's own existence and explicit per-invariant statement, per its own How-to-verify.

INV-7 (no SQL string interpolation): APPLIES (Ecto in use project-wide). `grep -rn 'Repo.query' lib/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard.ex` = no hits. No SQL of any kind in this module.

INV-8 (no unhandled crashes on realistic failure paths): APPLIES -- this is this diff's core subject matter. Verified by reading the real code (not the design's claim): read/4 and write/4 both call `Wasmex.Memory.size/2` fresh on every invocation (lines 132, 156 -- a local variable freshly bound each call, never a module attribute or cached state), then `check_bounds/3` runs BEFORE any Wasmex.Memory accessor call (the `case check_bounds(...) do :ok -> ... {:error, defect} -> ... end` wrapper at lines 134-143 and 159-168 means read_binary/4 and write_binary/4 are only reached inside the `:ok` branch) -- no code path reaches a live Wasmex.Memory call with unvalidated offset/length. Both call sites pattern-match the documented success shape AND an explicit `{:error, reason}` tuple (lines 136-138: `{:error, reason} -> ...; binary when is_binary(binary) -> {:ok, binary}`; lines 161-164: `{:error, reason} -> ...; :ok -> :ok`) -- exhaustive over every shape §1.6 found `Wasmex.Memory`'s own (incomplete) @specs could actually return; no unguarded `{:ok, x} = ...`-style match exists anywhere in the file (`grep -n '^\s*{:ok, .*} = ' lib/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard.ex` = no hits). check_bounds/3's arithmetic (lines 89-114) uses plain `+`/`>` on Elixir integers throughout -- no native-sized coercion, no `Bitwise`/`rem`/`Integer.mod` or any operation that could truncate a bignum -- so `range_end = offset + length` is exact at every magnitude tested (verified against 2^63-scale literals in the test file).

Design-vs-table discrepancy (ELIXIR-DEV-flagged): confirmed genuinely benign, independently re-derived, not just accepted on report. Shipped check_bounds/3 runs, in order: check_type_and_sign(offset), check_type_and_sign(length), check_offset_range(offset, memory_size), then check_end_of_range(offset, length, memory_size) -- this is design section 2's algorithm exactly (step 1 type/sign guard for both fields, step 3 offset-range check, step 4 end-of-range check), confirming ELIXIR-DEV implemented the algorithm as literally specified, not the table. For check_bounds(2^63, 2^63, 65536): step 3 fires first (offset 2^63 > memory_size) yielding {:offset_out_of_range, ...}, not the table's {:length_exceeds_memory, ...} -- reproduced by inspection and confirmed by the actual test assertion at test/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard_test.exs:90-91. Proved no safety gap exists regardless of check order: the final accept path (step 5) requires BOTH check_offset_range and check_end_of_range to return :ok. Since length >= 0 is already guaranteed by step 1 having passed, offset <= offset+length always holds, so offset <= memory_size is a NECESSARY consequence of (offset+length) <= memory_size -- i.e. any input that would pass the end-of-range check must also pass the offset-range check. Swapping the order of these two checks therefore cannot change which inputs are ultimately accepted vs rejected; it can only change which specific error atom is reported when both would reject anyway. The design's own table entry is simply a documentation-only worked-example error (it names the wrong of two simultaneously-true rejection reasons for that one input), not an algorithm defect -- verified independently, not merely accepted from ELIXIR-DEV's self-report.

Live-magnitude test-safety re-verification (independent, not trusting self-report): read every literal argument in test/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard_test.exs. The only >=2^40-scale values (9_223_372_036_854_775_808 = 2^63, at lines 87-88 and 96) are passed exclusively to `MemoryGuard.check_bounds/3` (a pure function, zero Wasmex/NIF dependency) -- never to `read/4`, `write/4`, or any `Wasmex.Memory.*` function. Every T3 live test (lines 118-164) uses only `size`, `size + 1000`, `size - 1`, `size + 1` -- all within a few thousand bytes of the real ~65536-byte fixture memory size, nowhere near the ~2^40 SIGABRT threshold §1.4 disclosed. No live-magnitude safety violation exists.

Independent verification run directly (not just re-reading ELIXIR-DEV's quoted output): `mix compile --warnings-as-errors` -- clean, no warnings. `mix test test/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard_test.exs` -- 'Result: 15 passed', 0 failures, matching ELIXIR-DEV's self-report exactly. `grep -rn 'Wasmex.Memory\.' lib/ --include='*.ex'` -- all 11 hits are inside lib/letflow/engine/wasm/memory_guard.ex itself (moduledoc prose plus the module's own size/2, read_binary/4, write_binary/4 call sites); no other file in lib/ references Wasmex.Memory, confirming AC1's single-validation-path claim independently.

Verdict: PASS. No BLOCKER found on any applicable invariant (INV-3, INV-4, INV-7, INV-8 all satisfied; INV-1/2/5 not-applicable, scope test explicitly run; INV-6 satisfied by this handoff). Routes next to REVIEWER per WF-02 Step 2c's gate sequence.
